positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter, a psychiatry resident, states the two-axis framework does not appropriately capture the risk of GenAI-enabled software functions, and points to prior instances and court cases involving generative AI providing false information as evidence that risk from medical advice must be defined objectively.
positions.requested_fda_action: Develop clear and objective methods for assessing the risk of any medical advice generated by GenAI-enabled functions, rather than relying on the proposed two-axis framework as described.
positions.public_summary: A resident physician in psychiatry states the proposed two-axis framework does not adequately capture GenAI software risk, citing past cases of generative AI providing false information, and calls for clear, objective methods for assessing the risk of medical advice.
positions.source_passage:
It does not appropriately capture the risk related to the Gen-AI enabled software
function.As a resident physician in the psychiatry space, it is imperative that we
are able to define clear and objective methods for the risk of the anything medical
advice made. Clearly we have always had several cases of issues and court
cases where the generativeAI is indicated and gave false information.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that action-directing outputs conveying any medical knowledge or guidance may be relied upon without users understanding the continued need for human mental health professionals, including therapists, counselors, and hotline specialists, not only physicians.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that action-directing GenAI functions involving any medical knowledge or guidance carry a clear message to users, addressed to patients and to non-physician mental health providers, emphasizing continued reliance on human professionals rather than an AI model.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on users substituting an AI model for human mental health professionals, raising the question of how much clinical role and authority is effectively handed to the device.

positions.public_summary: Commenter urges that action-directing outputs involving any medical knowledge or guidance carry clear messaging, directed to patients and to non-physician providers such as therapists, counselors, and hotline staff, stressing continued reliance on human mental health professionals rather than AI models.
positions.source_passage:
For a
action-directing function a clear message involving ANY kind of medical
knowledge or guidance needs to be put and not just for physicians, but for
therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, etc. Patient or people need to
understand and realize that it is imperative and important to continue to use US
in the mental health field versus an AI model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter raises concerns about the training data underlying generative AI models, stating that models are limited by what can be said and must be trained on patient or physician data, and that privacy and ethics would require everything to be consented. The commenter states uncertainty about how generative AI is developed and suggests that, because such models already use so much data, training to a full-consent standard would be impossible without ethical implications, referencing OpenEvidence AI.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific FDA action is requested in the passage; the commenter raises unresolved questions about consent, privacy, and ethics in the data used to train generative AI models.
positions.public_summary: Commenter raises concerns that generative AI models must be trained on patient or physician data, that privacy and ethics would require consent for all such data, and expresses uncertainty that existing large-scale models could meet that standard. No specific regulatory action requested.
positions.source_passage:
One the model is limited in the
space of what actually can be said and given, and has to be trained using patient
data or physician data. To maintain the privacy and ethics of healthcare-
everything would be consented too. Unsure how the generativeAI is done and
since it has already has some much data that is used, it would be impossible to
train the AI to this criteria without some ethical implications. Even
OpenevidenceAI.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that users and patients may treat generative AI outputs as failsafe, and that behavioral health settings in particular need assurances that patient safety is addressed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require disclaimers wherever AI-derived outputs are delivered—at drug administration points, clinics, and to individual users—stating that AI is not failsafe and results may vary, and ensure appropriate mental health facilities and clinics are involved in the behavioral health space.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The commenter frames the safeguard as a disclosure obligation applied at every site of use—clinics, administration points, and end users—rather than a premarket device-level requirement.

positions.public_summary: Commenter does not state a clear position on FDA's directiveness framework but urges that any AI-derived output carry disclaimers, at every clinic and point of use, that AI is not failsafe and results may vary, with added safeguards in behavioral health settings.
positions.source_passage:
In terms of the additional information- every drug administration, every health clinic, hell
everyone that uses the drug would need to have a disclaimer that makes note that
generative AI or AI in general is not a fail safe and that your results may vary. Anything
and everything would need to be said with the behavioural health space that appropriate
mental health facilities and clinics needed to be conducted to ensure PATIENTS that
their safety is represented.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's brief remark focuses on accessibility of AI-generated information for patients, indicating that outputs should be available in multiple languages and in simplified or alternative formats. The passage does not state a view on FDA's risk framing itself.
positions.requested_fda_action: Appears to ask that patient-facing GenAI outputs, in whatever form they are delivered, be translated into different languages and broken down into more accessible formats.
positions.public_summary: Fragmentary comment addressing patient-facing outputs, suggesting that AI-provided information should be translated into multiple languages and broken down into simpler or alternative formats. The passage does not indicate a clear position on FDA's proposed risk framing.
positions.source_passage:
In exposing on this question, in every form that the AI is provided- we would need to
have it translated into different languages and even broken down to the form.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that AI, despite seeming effective, creates more work than it saves and frustrates users much like automated phone systems, and says it is unclear how such tools would be implemented or audited in the mental health space; energy use is also cited as a reason for objection.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter asks that these tools not be implemented, asserting that patients across ages, sizes, and races also do not want them.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment frames the harm as added workload and user frustration in real-world use rather than as an incorrect device output.

positions.public_summary: An individual commenter opposes deployment of these tools generally, saying AI creates more work than it saves, frustrates users like automated phone systems, has unclear implementation and audit pathways in mental health care, and raises energy concerns. No specific FDA question is substantively addressed.
positions.source_passage:
Truthfully at the end of the day, with the idea of AI seemed really effective
and helpful, it is more work than anything. The same way that automated phone system
drive everyone crazy, so does AI. In terms of audits, mental health space, I have no
idea how this would be implemented. Surely from the energy standpoint, I DO NOT
want this implemented and neither do patients of all age size and race.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter asserts that generative AI cannot protect privacy because information transmitted over the internet is not secure, and that no currently available safeguard can mitigate the resulting risks.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require clear warnings that AI is being used and that privacy is not protected, and retain humans in the process rather than relying on technical safeguards to mitigate risk.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The commenter argues that retaining humans in the process is the only effective mitigation, framing safety as dependent on human involvement rather than device safeguards.
gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment treats data privacy and internet exposure as an unmitigable risk of GenAI-enabled functions, an issue not framed within FDA's risk questions.

positions.public_summary: Commenter argues no current safeguard can mitigate GenAI privacy risks because internet-transmitted information is not protected. Urges explicit disclosure that AI is in use and that privacy is not assured, and maintains that retaining humans is the only effective mitigation.
positions.source_passage:
Again a clear warning that AI does not protect
privacy because nothing on the internet is protected, and clear implication that AI is
being used. No safeguard currently can migrate risk and the only way to fix these risks
would to still have humans in place

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter describes personal experience with a generative AI clinical information tool that has increasingly responded that certain questions are out of its scope, while noting that nothing prevents physicians or medical students from seeking those answers elsewhere; the commenter reports having stopped using the tool.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific regulatory action is stated in the passage; the commenter only recounts experience with scope limitations and eventual discontinuation of use.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment observes that a tool's refusal to answer out-of-scope questions does not stop users from pursuing those queries elsewhere, touching on the boundary between declared scope and actual use behavior.

positions.public_summary: An individual commenter recounts that a generative AI clinical information tool increasingly declines questions as out of scope, notes users may seek answers elsewhere, and reports discontinuing use. No explicit regulatory position or recommendation is stated.
positions.source_passage:
Over
time, it has improved limitations of certain questions, reading the message that
Openevidence AI that the question is out of the scope, but who is not the stop other
physician or medical students to use it elsewhere. In the end, I have just stopped using
it

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter rejects the idea that trade-offs between error directions can be acceptable depending on clinical context, arguing that AI currently carries more risk and that manufacturer disclaimers do not shield anyone involved in deploying AI from responsibility, including government.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not accept context-dependent trade-offs in evaluating GenAI errors; hold all participants in AI use accountable rather than allowing responsibility to be shifted through disclaimers, consistent with a 'do no harm' standard.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asserts that everyone participating in AI use, including manufacturers who issue disclaimers and government bodies, bears responsibility for resulting harms.

positions.public_summary: A commenter, writing as a physician, rejects FDA's premise that acceptable trade-offs between under- and over-escalation vary by clinical context. Arguing AI currently carries more risk, the commenter states manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility from any party involved in AI use.
positions.source_passage:
Manufactures can put their disclaimer, but in the end, anyone that
participates in the use of AI in this space bares reasonability. The government system
itself, no one is immune to the consequences that will come with it. There are no
acceptable trade-offs by a clinical context. As a physician the oath comes into play: do
no harm, and since right now AI carries more risk and more reasonability

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter says the competency-based approach 'seems ideal in hindsight' but questions how patient safety and patient data would be maintained while it is carried out, and who bears responsibility if data are leaked.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not request a specific action; it asks FDA to address how patient safety and data protection would be maintained under the approach and who would be accountable in the event of a data leak.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment links data protection and potential leaks directly to patient safety, an angle not framed in the competency-based evaluation question.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asks who would be responsible if patient data were leaked, raising an unresolved allocation-of-responsibility issue.

positions.public_summary: Commenter finds the competency-based approach seemingly ideal but raises unanswered questions about how patient safety and data would be protected during its use, and who would be held responsible if patient data were leaked. No specific position or change is stated.
positions.source_passage:
The approach seems ideal in hindsight, but how will one maintain patient
safety and data during this? Who is not to say that the data gets leaked anyway, and in
that case who is responsible?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states the two-axis risk framework is unnecessary because HIPAA and the Security Rule already govern privacy and security obligations for healthcare providers, and questions how patient data will be kept from being breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter asks FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians to explain and ensure how patient data will be protected against breach, theft, or sale, rather than adopting the proposed two-axis risk framework.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment frames patient data breach, theft, or sale as the central risk concern, which FDA's two-axis framing of device activity and consequence of incorrect output does not address.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, physicians, and other healthcare colleagues will collectively ensure data protection, implying responsibility is spread across multiple parties.

positions.public_summary: This commenter rejects the proposed two-axis risk framework as unnecessary, asserting that HIPAA and the Security Rule already impose uniform privacy and security duties, and instead asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians will prevent patient data breach, theft, or sale.
positions.source_passage:
The two-axis framework is not even needed. Currently HIPPA laws and the
Security Rule of Healthcare govern that all healthcare providers within the space must
follow the same privacy and security that all would want--- how will the FDA,
government, manufactures, and physicians and other healthcare colleagues ensure that
patient data will be protected and not breached or stolen or sold?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the proposed benchmarking structure favorably but does not consider it sufficient on its own, arguing that a clinical trial or study is also needed, and raises unresolved questions about informed consent and safeguarding patient confidentiality while the device delivers accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require clinical trial or study evidence in addition to benchmarking, and address how informed consent and patient confidentiality would be handled in the evaluation framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter finds the proposed benchmarking structure acceptable but insufficient alone, stating a clinical trial or study would also be needed. Raises unaddressed questions about informed consent and how patient confidentiality would be maintained while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.source_passage:
The benchmarking structure is nice, but a clinical trial or study would need to
be done and the idea of informed consent would have to be discussed. In essence as
well how does that maintain that patient confidentiality will be paramount while
delivering accurate and clinically appropriate data/info?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states they cannot answer how benchmark performance would predict real-world behavior because the benchmarking concept is underdeveloped, and notes that behavioral health involves greater nuance and more serious consequences when outputs are wrong. They also question who bears responsibility for patient safety and informed consent under federal law.
positions.requested_fda_action: Further develop and clearly specify the benchmarking approach and validate it through a pilot study, including a separate study addressing behavioral health, and clarify who is accountable for patient safety and informed consent.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asks who is responsible for patient safety and informed consent, and notes federal legal consequences, an allocation question not addressed by the benchmark-validity question.

positions.public_summary: Commenter cannot answer FDA's benchmark validity question, saying the benchmarking concept needs further development and should be tested through a pilot study, with a separate study for behavioral health given its nuance and consequences. Also asks who bears responsibility for patient safety and informed consent.
positions.source_passage:
No idea- again this benchmark really needs more fleshing out and there
would need to be a pilot study with the idea clearly laid out to be done. Also a
behavioral health study- our field is much more nuance and have more of a greater idea
and consequence if something were to go wrong. Again in terms of patient safety and
informed consent- who is responsible? These are federal laws and with them come
federal consequences.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to allowing clinical confirmation without a prospective clinical study, characterizing less rigorous alternatives as cutting corners, and also raises a concern about public transparency.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial study for clinical confirmation of GenAI-enabled devices and make the results clear and publicly available.
positions.public_summary: Opposes FDA's suggestion that clinical confirmation might not always require a prospective clinical study, describing such flexibility as cutting corners. Calls for clinical trial studies and for results to be made clear to everyone, including the public.
positions.source_passage:
No, don’t cut corners- do a clinical trial study and make it clear to everyone
including the public. THAT is not ok.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage is a fragmentary note mentioning survey-based (Qualtrics) studies, accuracy of information provided, and patient information, with an unspecified reservation about informed consent. No developed argument or position can be identified.
positions.requested_fda_action: No discernible request to FDA is stated in the passage.
positions.public_summary: Fragmentary comment referencing survey-based studies, accuracy of information provided, and patient information, while noting an unspecified concern about informed consent. The passage does not state a clear position or request regarding FDA's proposals.
positions.source_passage:
Qualtrics studies, accuracy of info given, patient info- but again dicey with
the informed consent

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that many groups—patients generally, and specifically behavioral health, elderly, pediatric, non-English-speaking, low-socioeconomic-status, and rural populations—may be unable to participate well in evaluation studies, and states they do not know how full inclusiveness could be achieved. They note that if the study population is limited, the resulting data are limited.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not state a specific requested action; it raises the concern that evaluation evidence will be limited unless studies include hard-to-reach subpopulations such as behavioral health, elderly, pediatric, non-English-speaking, low-socioeconomic, and rural patients.
positions.public_summary: Commenter raises concerns about subpopulation representativeness in evaluation, noting patients—particularly behavioral health, elderly, pediatric, non-English-speaking, lower-socioeconomic, and rural groups—may not participate well, and that limited studies yield limited data. No specific alternative approach or FDA action is proposed.
positions.source_passage:
Almost everyone. Patients are the most likely to not understand something.
Behavioral health, elderly, children, patients in different languages and socioeconomic
factors may not be able to participate in this study well, rural populations. No idea how
one would be inclusive for all but If the study is limited, the data is limited in my position.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter doubts that a panel of qualified clinicians can realistically serve as the performance comparator, because in their experience few physicians would agree to participate out of fear of professional backlash, society scrutiny, and risk to their personal safety and medical license.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not offer an alternative, but suggests any clinician-panel comparator would require willing qualified clinicians and might have to be arranged through a hospital; they signal FDA should reconsider reliance on clinician panels given recruitment and liability barriers.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter raises that individual clinicians serving as evaluators bear personal professional and licensure exposure for judgments used in device evaluation, a burden FDA's question does not address.

positions.public_summary: Commenter questions the feasibility of using clinician panels as the performance comparator for open-ended outputs, saying few physicians would agree to participate due to fear of professional backlash and risk to their licenses, though no alternative comparator is proposed.
positions.source_passage:
I don’t believe this would make sense either, and again don’t have a answer
here. There would need to be qualified clinicians that would have to agree – maybe it
could be done with the hospital- but despite many physicians using AI I don’t know
many that would agree to actually participating in it for fear of the backlash, the society
and again the safety of themselves and their only license.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the question cannot be meaningfully answered without a comparative device and a pilot study, and rejects each of FDA's suggested alternative comparators: unaided clinical judgment would make the study pointless, delayed specialist review would only delay care, and while 'no intervention' may be an appropriate comparator, the commenter questions who determines that it is justified when the output comes from a machine rather than a person.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not rely on the alternative comparators described (unaided clinical judgment or delayed specialist review); establish comparative device data and pilot studies as the basis for comparison, and clarify who validates a 'no intervention' comparator when the determination originates from a machine rather than a clinician.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The commenter questions whether a 'no intervention' course of action can be considered justified when it is generated by a machine rather than decided by a person, raising who holds authority to validate such determinations.

positions.public_summary: Commenter says the comparator question is not answerable without a comparative device and pilot study. Rejects unaided clinical judgment (would negate the study's purpose) and delayed specialist review (delays care). Accepts 'no intervention' as possible, but questions who validates machine-originated determinations.
positions.source_passage:
Not really answerable at this time, we would need a comparative device and
a pilot study to really have something to compare it too.
No unaided clinical judgement, like why bother doing the study at all. Delayed specialist
review would only delay care, which is dumb. No intervention must be an appropriate
answer but since it is due by a robot and not a person- who is say that it is justified?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that an independent third party should be created with broad participation from research boards, NIH, mental health organizations (e.g., NAMI, SAMHSA), and the AMA, arguing accurate results and support would otherwise not be obtained, but then states such involvement would not be possible. Privacy and data protection are named as constraints on design features.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish an independent third-party body drawing on research review boards, federal health agencies, professional and mental health organizations, while addressing privacy and data protection limits; the commenter simultaneously doubts such participation is feasible.
positions.public_summary: Commenter suggests an independent third party formed with research boards, NIH, mental health organizations, and the AMA is needed for accurate results, while also stating such involvement may not be possible, and cites privacy and data protection as constraints. Position internally inconsistent.
positions.source_passage:
An independent third-party would be create. All of the research boards, the
national institute of health, the mental health organizations like NAMI and SAMHSA,
AMA everyone should be involved. You wouldn’t get accurate results or information or
even support otherwise. I don’t think that third-party involvements of these above
organizations would be possible. Limiting design features is again privacy and data
protection.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the competency-based approach appealing but is concerned that the discussion paper and its questions are written in technical language and appear to have been generated with AI, limiting meaningful public input.
positions.requested_fda_action: Before advancing the competency-based approach, FDA should solicit input from a wider range of groups and from the general public, including through a version of the material written in more accessible, comparable terms.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports the competency-based approach in principle but asks FDA to first broaden consultation, seeking input from multiple groups and the general public through materials written in more accessible language rather than the paper's current technical framing.
positions.source_passage:
I like the competency based approach but first yall need to flesh out the
public’s opinion on this in addition to generative AI- which it seems wrote these
responses. Reaching out to several different groups with these questions as well
involving the public’s opinion on this with a research paper that is written in more similar
terms would be ideal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter raises privacy and ethics concerns about the patient and physician data used to train generative AI models, suggesting that consent would be required for all such data, and expresses doubt that existing models (citing OpenEvidence AI as an example) could be trained to such a standard given the volume of data already used.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific regulatory action is requested; the passage suggests that model outputs be constrained in what can be said and that training data be consented, while questioning whether that is achievable for already-trained models.
positions.public_summary: Brief, informal comment raising privacy and consent concerns about patient and physician data used to train generative AI models, and doubting that already-trained models such as OpenEvidence AI could meet a full-consent standard. No clear position on FDA's proposals.
positions.source_passage: ne the model is limited in the space of what actually can be said and given, and has to be trained using patient data or physician data. To maintain the privacy and ethics of healthcare- everything would be consented too. Unsure how the generativeAI is done and since it has already has some much data that is used, it would be impossible to train the AI to this criteria without some ethical implications. Even OpenevidenceAI.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that patients and other non-physician users may rely on generative AI outputs conveying medical knowledge or guidance in place of human mental health professionals.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that action-directing functions delivering any medical knowledge or guidance carry a clear message—directed not only to physicians but to therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, and patients—that human professionals should continue to be used in the mental health field rather than an AI model.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges that any action-directing generative AI function conveying medical knowledge or guidance include clear messaging—for patients and for therapists, counselors, and hotline staff—emphasizing continued reliance on human mental health professionals rather than an AI model.
positions.source_passage: Response: For a action-directing function a clear message involving ANY kind of medical knowledge or guidance needs to be put and not just for physicians, but for therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, etc. Patient or people need to understand and realize that it is imperative and important to continue to use US in the mental health field versus an AI model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that AI, despite seeming effective, creates more work and is frustrating in the way automated phone systems are, and says they do not know how it would be implemented for audits in the mental health space. They also object on energy grounds and assert that patients do not want it either.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not request a specific regulatory action but states they do not want this implemented.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The commenter's core claim is that AI adds workload and user frustration rather than clinical benefit, a workflow-level harm not addressed by the paper's output-accuracy framing.

positions.public_summary: An individual commenter opposes implementation, saying AI creates more work and frustration comparable to automated phone systems, questions how it would be applied to audits in mental health, and objects on energy grounds. No specific FDA action is requested.
positions.source_passage: Response: Truthfully at the end of the day, with the idea of AI seemed really effective and helpful, it is more work than anything. The same way that automated phone system drive everyone crazy, so does AI. In terms of audits, mental health space, I have no idea how this would be implemented. Surely from the energy standpoint, I DO NOT want this implemented and neither do patients of all age size and race.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A clinician user reports that a widely used generative AI clinical reference tool has expanded into functions such as handling patient messages, which the commenter considers inappropriate, and observes that although the tool sometimes declines out-of-scope questions, nothing prevents physicians or medical students from using it outside its stated scope; the commenter states they have stopped using it.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not state a specific requested FDA action; it conveys concern about expanding product functionality and the absence of any effective constraint on use beyond the tool's declared scope.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The commenter notes that in-product out-of-scope refusal messages do not prevent clinicians or students from using the tool for purposes outside its declared scope, and that the product's functions have expanded over time.

positions.public_summary: A clinician user criticizes a generative AI clinical reference tool's expansion into patient-message and privacy-related functions and notes that out-of-scope refusal messages do not prevent use beyond the tool's stated scope. The comment states no explicit position on FDA's proposals.
positions.source_passage: The model that currently seems to work for many clinicians with a valid NPI number is OpenEvidence AI. While many of us use it to help write prior authorizations and look up new and updating criteria, the idea of physicians using it for patients privacy, messages, etc that is now on the site is RIDICULOUS and frankly an insult to my intelligence. Over time, it has improved limitations of certain questions, reading the message that Openevidence AI that the question is out of the scope, but who is not the stop other physician or medical students to use it elsewhere. In the end, I have just stopped using it

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter rejects the premise that trade-offs between under- and over-escalation can be acceptable depending on clinical context, invoking the physician obligation to do no harm and asserting that AI currently carries more risk. The commenter also states that manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility, and that everyone participating in AI use, including government, bears responsibility and consequences.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not treat error trade-offs as acceptable based on clinical context, and ensure responsibility is not shifted through manufacturer disclaimers but shared by all parties involved in deploying AI.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asserts that manufacturer disclaimers do not limit liability and that all participants in AI use, including clinicians and government, bear responsibility for consequences.

positions.public_summary: Commenter rejects FDA's premise that escalation error trade-offs can be acceptable and context-dependent, citing the physician duty to do no harm and asserting AI currently carries greater risk. Argues manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility, which is shared by all participants.
positions.source_passage: Response: Manufactures can put their disclaimer, but in the end, anyone that participates in the use of AI in this space bares reasonability. The government system itself, no one is immune to the consequences that will come with it. There are no  acceptable trade-offs by a clinical context. As a physician the oath comes into play: do no harm, and since right now AI carries more risk and more reasonability

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the competency-based approach appealing in principle but questions how patient safety and patient data would be protected while benchmarking and clinical confirmation are carried out, and who bears responsibility if data is leaked.
positions.requested_fda_action: Address how patient data protection and safety would be maintained under a competency-based evaluation approach, and clarify who is accountable in the event of a data breach.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment frames data leakage during device evaluation as a patient safety and data protection concern not addressed by the competency-based framework question.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter explicitly asks who would be responsible if patient data is leaked, indicating unresolved allocation of accountability.

positions.public_summary: Commenter views the competency-based approach as appealing in principle but questions how patient safety and patient data would be safeguarded during benchmarking and clinical confirmation, and asks FDA to clarify who is responsible if data is leaked.
positions.source_passage: Response: The approach seems ideal in hindsight, but how will one maintain patient safety and data during this? Who is not to say that the data gets leaked anyway, and in that case who is responsible?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter asserts the two-axis risk framework is unnecessary because HIPAA and the Healthcare Security Rule already impose uniform privacy and security obligations on providers, and instead questions how patient data will be kept from being breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.requested_fda_action: Set aside the proposed two-axis risk framework and instead address how FDA, government, manufacturers, physicians, and other healthcare personnel will collectively ensure patient data is protected from breach, theft, or sale.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The commenter treats patient data breach, theft, or sale as the central risk concern rather than the output-reliance risks FDA's two-axis framework addresses.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, physicians, and other healthcare colleagues will jointly ensure data protection, implying responsibility is spread across multiple actors without a clear locus.

positions.public_summary: Commenter rejects the two-axis risk framework as unnecessary, arguing existing HIPAA and Security Rule obligations already apply, and instead asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians will jointly ensure patient data is not breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.source_passage: Response: The two-axis framework is not even needed. Currently HIPPA laws and the Security Rule of Healthcare govern that all healthcare providers within the space must follow the same privacy and security that all would want--- how will the FDA, government, manufactures, and physicians and other healthcare colleagues ensure that patient data will be protected and not breached or stolen or sold?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the proposed benchmarking structure as acceptable but not sufficient on its own, and raises unaddressed questions about informed consent and safeguarding patient confidentiality while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial or study in addition to benchmarking, and address informed consent and patient confidentiality protections as part of the evaluation framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter finds the benchmarking structure acceptable but says it alone is insufficient, urging that a clinical trial or study also be conducted. Raises unresolved questions about informed consent and maintaining patient confidentiality while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.source_passage: Response: The benchmarking structure is nice, but a clinical trial or study would need to be done and the idea of informed consent would have to be discussed. In essence as well how does that maintain that patient confidentiality will be paramount while delivering accurate and clinically appropriate data/info?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states they cannot answer how benchmark validity would be established because the benchmarking concept is not sufficiently developed, and notes that behavioral health involves greater nuance and more serious consequences when outputs are wrong. They also raise unresolved questions about who bears responsibility for patient safety and informed consent under federal law.
positions.requested_fda_action: Flesh out the benchmarking approach in greater detail and test it through a clearly specified pilot study, including a study specific to behavioral health. Clarify who is accountable for patient safety and informed consent.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter asks who is responsible for patient safety and informed consent under federal law, an accountability question not addressed by the benchmark validity question as framed.

positions.public_summary: Commenter says the benchmarking proposal is too underdeveloped to evaluate, calling for a clearly specified pilot study and a behavioral health-specific study given that field's nuance and consequences. Also asks FDA to clarify responsibility for patient safety and informed consent.
positions.source_passage: Response: No idea- again this benchmark really needs more fleshing out and there would need to be a pilot study with the idea clearly laid out to be done. Also a behavioral health study- our field is much more nuance and have more of a greater idea and consequence if something were to go wrong. Again in terms of patient safety and informed consent- who is responsible? These are federal laws and with them come federal consequences.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to allowing clinical confirmation without a prospective clinical study, characterizing flexible confirmation approaches as cutting corners, and also expresses concern about transparency to the public.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial study for clinical confirmation and make the process and results clear to everyone, including the public.
positions.public_summary: The commenter opposes FDA's suggestion that clinical confirmation of GenAI-enabled devices may not always require a prospective clinical study, stating that a clinical trial should be conducted and that the process and findings should be made clear to the public.
positions.source_passage: Response: No, don’t cut corners- do a clinical trial study and make it clear to everyone including the public. THAT is not ok.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage is a fragmentary note suggesting survey-based (Qualtrics) studies and measurement of the accuracy of information provided, while flagging that collecting or using patient information raises unresolved informed consent difficulties.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific action is articulated; the note implies that survey-type studies and accuracy measures could be used as evidence, but that informed consent issues around patient information would need to be addressed.
positions.public_summary: A brief, fragmentary note suggesting survey-based (Qualtrics) studies and measurement of information accuracy as possible evidence approaches, while flagging that use of patient information raises unresolved informed consent difficulties. No clear position on FDA's proposal is stated.
positions.source_passage: Response: Qualtrics studies, accuracy of info given, patient info- but again dicey with the informed consent

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that many groups—patients generally, behavioral health populations, the elderly, children, non-English speakers, lower-socioeconomic and rural populations—may be unable to participate well in evaluation studies, and states that a limited study yields limited data.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not specify a requested action; it implies evaluation should account for populations that cannot readily participate, while acknowledging uncertainty about how to be inclusive of all groups.
positions.public_summary: Commenter notes that many groups—patients broadly, behavioral health, elderly, children, non-English speakers, lower-income and rural populations—may not participate well in evaluation studies, and that limited studies produce limited data. No specific regulatory recommendation or clear stance is stated.
positions.source_passage: Response: Almost everyone. Patients are the most likely to not understand something. Behavioral health, elderly, children, patients in different languages and socioeconomic factors may not be able to participate in this study well, rural populations. No idea how one would be inclusive for all but If the study is limited, the data is limited in my position.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter doubts that using a panel of qualified clinicians as the performance comparator is workable, stating that few physicians they know would agree to participate out of fear of backlash, professional society reaction, and risk to their personal safety and medical license.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter offers no alternative approach, but implies FDA should not rely on clinician-panel comparators without addressing clinician willingness to participate and the professional and licensure exposure such participation may create; involvement through hospitals is raised only as a possibility.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment raises individual clinicians' personal licensure and reputational exposure as a barrier to their serving in device evaluation roles, an accountability question FDA's comparator question does not address.

positions.public_summary: Commenter doubts that a clinician panel can serve as a workable performance comparator, saying few physicians would agree to participate given fear of backlash, professional society reaction, and risk to their license. Suggests hospital involvement as a possibility but offers no alternative.
positions.source_passage: Response: I don’t believe this would make sense either, and again don’t have a answer here. There would need to be qualified clinicians that would have to agree – maybe it could be done with the hospital- but despite many physicians using AI I don’t know many that would agree to actually participating in it for fear of the backlash, the society and again the safety of themselves and their only license.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the comparator question cannot be meaningfully answered without a comparative device and pilot data, and rejects each of the alternative comparators FDA describes: unaided clinical judgment would defeat the purpose of the study, delayed specialist review would only delay care, and while 'no intervention' may be appropriate, the commenter questions who determines it is justified when the output comes from a machine rather than a person.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not endorse the alternative comparators suggested in Q15 and implies that comparator selection should await evidence from a comparative device and pilot study; the commenter also asks who would justify a 'no intervention' comparator when the determination is machine-generated.
positions.public_summary: Commenter says the comparator question is not answerable without a comparative device and pilot study, and rejects FDA's suggested alternatives: unaided clinical judgment would negate the study, delayed specialist review would delay care, and 'no intervention' raises questions about who justifies a machine-generated determination.
positions.source_passage:
Response: Not really answerable at this time, we would need a comparative device and a pilot study to really have something to compare it too.
No unaided clinical judgement, like why bother doing the study at all. Delayed specialist review would only delay care, which is dumb. No intervention must be an appropriate answer but since it is due by a robot and not a person- who is say that it is justified?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that broad independent third-party involvement (research boards, NIH, mental health organizations such as NAMI and SAMHSA, and the AMA) is necessary because accurate results, information, or support would not otherwise be obtained, while simultaneously doubting that such involvement of these organizations would be possible.
positions.requested_fda_action: Involve a wide range of independent bodies — research review boards, NIH, mental health organizations, and professional associations — in third-party assessment, and treat privacy and data protection as the key limiting design consideration.
positions.public_summary: Commenter endorses involving many independent bodies (research boards, NIH, NAMI, SAMHSA, AMA) in third-party assessment, arguing accurate results otherwise are unobtainable, but also doubts such involvement would be feasible, and identifies privacy and data protection as the limiting design consideration.
positions.source_passage: Response: An independent third-party would be create. All of the research boards, the national institute of health, the mental health organizations like NAMI and SAMHSA, AMA everyone should be involved. You wouldn’t get accurate results or information or even support otherwise. I don’t think that third-party involvements of these above organizations would be possible. Limiting design features is again privacy and data protection.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter likes the competency-based approach in principle but is concerned that the discussion paper and its questions appear to have been drafted with generative AI and are not accessible to non-specialist audiences, and that public input has not been adequately gathered.
positions.requested_fda_action: Solicit broader input by reaching out to multiple different groups and the general public, including through a version of the paper written in plainer, more comparable terms, before advancing the competency-based approach.
positions.public_summary: Commenter expresses general support for the competency-based approach but asks FDA to first gather broader public and multi-group input, including through materials written in plainer language, noting concern that the discussion paper's questions appear to be generative AI-drafted.
positions.source_passage: Response; I like the competency based approach but first yall need to flesh out the public’s opinion on this in addition to generative AI- which it seems wrote these responses. Reaching out to several different groups with these questions as well involving the public’s opinion on this with a research paper that is written in more similar terms would be ideal.
